chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Suleiman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyas, who said:

I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying regarding a man who caught the Friday prayer and the people were crowded, so he said Takbir with the Imam and bowed (Ruku'), and he was unable to prostrate (Sujood). The Imam stood up while the people were in the second Raka'ah, and this man stood with them. The Imam bowed, and this man was unable to bow in the second Raka'ah due to the crowding, but he was able to prostrate. What should he do?

Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: As for the first Raka'ah, it is complete up to the Ruku'. Since he did not prostrate for it until he entered into the second, that was not sufficient for him. When he prostrated in the second Raka'ah, if he intended this prostration to be the first Raka'ah, then the first Raka'ah is complete for him. And when the Imam offers Salam, he should stand and pray one Raka'ah, then prostrate in it, then recite Tashahhud and offer Salam. And if he did not intend that that prostration was for the first Raka'ah, then neither the first nor the second is valid for him.
ai.seo_question: How is the Friday prayer validated if a person misses the first prostration due to crowd pressure?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of 'intention' (niyyah) in resolving structural defects (nuqs) in congregational prayer, specifically addressing the ambiguity of prostrations when physical constraints prevent standard sequence. It highlights the Shia juristic view that a single prostration can serve dual purposes if explicitly intended, thereby preserving the validity of the first Raka'ah and necessitating only a compensatory Raka'ah rather than a full repetition. This ruling underscores the flexibility within Shia fiqh to accommodate practical difficulties (shiddah) without invalidating the core act of worship.
